stops.name: Artaxata, the Armenian Carthage
stops.campa: The trail bends inland, to the court of Artaxias of Armenia, and here the destroyer becomes a founder. He sees an elbow of land in the Araxes, river-ringed but for a narrow isthmus, Ararat on the horizon like a witness, ground read by the same eye that read Cannae, and he persuades the king to set his capital there, and lays out the city himself. Artaxata rises on Hannibal's plan and is called the Armenian Carthage: the city of a man whose own city cast him out, planted at the earth's far end from Rome. Plutarch carries it, Strabo carries it, and the register builds the walls.

stops.name: Prusa, the court of Bithynia
stops.campa: The last court that will have him is the smallest: Prusias of Bithynia, a cautious king in a poor kingdom at war with Eumenes of Pergamon, Rome's favorite. Hannibal, near seventy, pays for his shelter in the only coin he has ever carried: victories. He directs the king's war, and in the quiet between campaigns founds a city for him at the foot of the Mysian Olympus: Prusa, which will live under that mountain for two thousand years. Two cities standing at opposite ends of the world, Artaxata and Prusa, are the exile's monuments: the man who could not save his own city kept building other people's.

stops.name: The Propontis, the serpent-pots of the Bithynian fleet
stops.campa: Outnumbered at sea by Pergamon, Hannibal fights his last battle with pottery. He has the country scoured for venomous snakes, sealed by the thousand into clay jars; then, to find the king among his ships, sends a herald with a letter under the caduceus: the letter is mere insult; its course marks the royal flagship. The order: every Bithynian ship converges on Eumenes alone; against the rest, the jars. The pots arc over the water and burst on the Pergamene decks; the sailors laugh, until the decks begin to move. Pergamon's fleet flees a rain of snakes, and the old man takes his last victory from the earth.

stops.name: Libyssa, the house of seven doors and the ring
stops.campa: Flamininus comes to Bithynia, and the cautious king weighs an old guest against Rome and chooses Rome. Soldiers close on the house at Libyssa. Hannibal, who has expected every betrayal since the first, built it with seven doors, but a runner from each returns with the same word: soldiers, at all of them. He calls for the poison carried for years beneath the stone of his ring, kept for this one unwatchable door; curses Prusias, calling hospitality's gods to witness the broken faith; speaks the last sentence, level as a ledger; and drinks. He is sixty-four. That same season Scipio dies in his own exile at Liternum.
stops.quote: Let us relieve the Roman people of their long anxiety, since they think it long to wait for the death of an old man.
stops.quote_source: Livy 39.51, liberemus diuturna cura populum Romanum

stops.name: The tumulus of Libyssa, the grave
stops.campa: They bury him where he fell, in a mound above the Gulf of Nicomedia, and Libyssa fades until, in Pliny's day, it is remembered for one thing: the tumulus of Hannibal. Tradition says Septimius Severus, the African-born emperor, faced the mound in white marble four centuries on. The exact spot slips from human knowledge, the canon's last honest gap, but travelers still seek it on the hillsides between Gebze and the water, where another soldier-founder of another republic ordered the grave honored again. The oath is discharged: nine years old at the altar, sixty-four at the ring, and never, not for one hour, a friend of Rome.
